claim: De novo lipogenesis is associated with the development of human diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and obesity.
source: De novo lipogenesis is associated with the development of human diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ameer et al., 2014 in the introduction section.

claim: Acetyl coenzyme A (CoA) plays a crucial role in fatty acid synthesis.
source: At the core of lipogenesis lies acetyl coenzyme A (CoA), a metabolite that plays a crucial role in fatty acid synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: SIRT2 catalyzes the deacetylation of ACSS2 at the lysine residue K271 when cells encounter nutrient stress, particularly a deficiency in amino acids.
source: Here, we reveal that when cells encounter nutrient stress, particularly a deficiency in amino acids, Sirtuin 2 (SIRT2) catalyzes the deacetylation of ACSS2 at the lysine residue K271.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including mass spectrometry and western blot analyses.

claim: K271 deacetylation results in K271 ubiquitination and subsequently proteasomal degradation of ACSS2.
source: This results in K271 ubiquitination and subsequently proteasomal degradation of ACSS2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing ubiquitination and degradation assays.

claim: Substitution of K271 leads to decreased ubiquitination of ACSS2.
source: Substitution of K271 leads to decreased ubiquitination of ACSS2, increased ACSS2 protein level, and thus increased lipogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing K271R mutant has decreased ubiquitination.

claim: Substitution of K271 leads to increased ACSS2 protein level.
source: Substitution of K271 leads to decreased ubiquitination of ACSS2, increased ACSS2 protein level, and thus increased lipogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing K271R mutant has higher protein levels.

claim: Substitution of K271 leads to increased lipogenesis.
source: Substitution of K271 leads to decreased ubiquitination of ACSS2, increased ACSS2 protein level, and thus increased lipogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data showing increased lipid accumulation.

claim: DNL underlies the pathogenesis of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and obesity.
source: DNL underlies the pathogenesis of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and obesity, and is also exacerbated in cancer (Ameer et al., 2014; Nassir et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ameer et al., 2014 and Nassir et al., 2015.

claim: DNL is exacerbated in cancer.
source: DNL underlies the pathogenesis of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and obesity, and is also exacerbated in cancer (Ameer et al., 2014; Nassir et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ameer et al., 2014 and Nassir et al., 2015.

claim: ACLY converts citrate derived from the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid cycle into acetyl-CoA for DNL.
source: One pathway is governed by the enzyme ATP citrate lyase (ACLY), which converts citrate derived from the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid cycle into acetyl-CoA for DNL (Icard et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Icard et al., 2020 and Feng et al., 2020.

claim: ACSS2 catalyzes the ligation of exogenous acetate to CoA, generating acetyl-CoA in an ATP-dependent reaction.
source: The second pathway involves acetyl-CoA synthetase 2 (ACSS2), which catalyzes the ligation of exogenous acetate to CoA, generating acetyl-CoA in an ATP-dependent reaction (Ling et al., 2022; Schug et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ling et al., 2022 and Schug et al., 2015.

claim: Acetate uptake increases under conditions of stress, such as low oxygen and nutrient availability.
source: While acetate is not typically a fuel source in mammalian cells, its uptake increases under conditions of stress, such as low oxygen and nutrient availability (Zhao, 2025; Schug et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhao, 2025 and Schug et al., 2016.

claim: ACSS2 promotes malignant cell growth by allowing cells to utilize acetate as an additional nutritional source when other carbon sources are scarce.
source: In the metabolically stressed tumor microenvironment, ACSS2 promotes malignant cell growth by allowing cells to utilize acetate as an additional nutritional source when other carbon sources are scarce (Schug et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schug et al., 2015, Miller et al., 2021, and Chen et al., 2015.

claim: ACSS2 has been found to be upregulated in various cancers, including breast and hepatic cancer.
source: Consequently, ACSS2 has been found to be upregulated in various cancers, including breast and hepatic cancer (Ling et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ling et al., 2022, Miller et al., 2021, and Gao et al., 2016.

claim: ACSS2 has been implicated in promoting the progression of hepatic steatosis.
source: Recent studies have implicated ACSS2 in promoting the progression of hepatic steatosis, a condition defined by aberrant fat build-up in the liver (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2018.

claim: Mice lacking ACSS2 exhibited a significant reduction in body weight, serum cholesterol, as well as lower hepatic triglyceride levels in a diet-induced obesity model.
source: In a diet-induced obesity model, mice lacking ACSS2 exhibited a significant reduction in body weight, serum cholesterol, as well as lower hepatic triglyceride levels (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2018.

claim: Most cytosolic and nuclear lysine acetylation is installed by a set of acetyltransferases, including p300/CBP, PCAF, and HAT1.
source: Most cytosolic and nuclear lysine acetylation is installed by a set of acetyltransferases, including p300/CBP, PCAF, and HAT1, while the enzymes for most mitochondrial lysine acetylation events remain unknown (Drazic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Drazic et al., 2016.

claim: The enzymes for most mitochondrial lysine acetylation events remain unknown.
source: Most cytosolic and nuclear lysine acetylation is installed by a set of acetyltransferases, including p300/CBP, PCAF, and HAT1, while the enzymes for most mitochondrial lysine acetylation events remain unknown (Drazic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Drazic et al., 2016.

claim: Lysine acetylation can be removed by members of the metal ion-dependent histone deacetylases (HDAC1-11) or NAD+-dependent sirtuin (SIRT1-SIRT7) family of enzymes.
source: Lysine acetylation is reversible and can be removed by members of the metal ion-dependent histone deacetylases (HDAC1-11) or NAD+-dependent sirtuin (SIRT1-SIRT7) family of enzymes (Park and Kim, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Park and Kim, 2020.

claim: The catalytic activity of ACSS2 was reported to be inhibited by lysine acetylation on K661.
source: The catalytic activity of ACSS2 was reported to be inhibited by lysine acetylation on K661 and activated by SIRT1-catalyzed deacetylation (Hallows et al., 2006; Sahar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hallows et al., 2006 and Sahar et al., 2014.

claim: The catalytic activity of ACSS2 is activated by SIRT1-catalyzed deacetylation.
source: The catalytic activity of ACSS2 was reported to be inhibited by lysine acetylation on K661 and activated by SIRT1-catalyzed deacetylation (Hallows et al., 2006; Sahar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hallows et al., 2006 and Sahar et al., 2014.

claim: ACSS2 undergoes deacetylation mediated by SIRT1.
source: Hallows et al. revealed that ACSS2 undergoes deacetylation mediated by SIRT1, a class III deacetylase (Hallows et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hallows et al., 2006.

claim: SIRT1 and SIRT2 are the major cytosolic members among the seven known class III deacetylases in mammalian cells.
source: Among the seven known class III deacetylases in mammalian cells (Sirt1-7), SIRT1 and SIRT2 are the major cytosolic members (Carafa et al., 2016; Imai and Guarente, 2014; Wang and Lin, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carafa et al., 2016, Imai and Guarente, 2014, and Wang and Lin, 2021.

claim: The expression of SIRT2 led to a decrease in ACSS2 acetylation.
source: Our results demonstrated that the expression of SIRT2 led to a decrease in ACSS2 acetylation, indicating that SIRT2 is capable of deacetylating ACSS2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SIRT2 is capable of deacetylating ACSS2.
source: Our results demonstrated that the expression of SIRT2 led to a decrease in ACSS2 acetylation, indicating that SIRT2 is capable of deacetylating ACSS2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing decreased acetylation upon SIRT2 expression.

claim: SIRT2 knockdown increased ACSS2 acetylation under nutrient stress.
source: This resulted in an increase in SIRT2 levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and when SIRT2 was knocked down under this condition, ACSS2 had increased acetylation compared to control knockdown cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The deacetylation of ACSS2 by SIRT2 happens in the context of nutrient stress.
source: These findings suggest that the deacetylation of ACSS2 by SIRT2 happens in the context of nutrient stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing SIRT2-dependent deacetylation only under nutrient stress conditions.

claim: SIRT2 is upregulated under conditions of low glucose or amino acid deprivation.
source: SIRT2 has been reported to be upregulated under various stress conditions, including Golgi stress induced by shigella infection (Wang et al., 2022; Zullo et al., 2018) as well as under conditions of low glucose or amino acid deprivation (Zullo et al., 2018; Wang and Tong, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zullo et al., 2018 and Wang and Tong, 2009.

claim: Under amino acid deprivation, SIRT2 knockdown increased ACSS2 acetylation levels.
source: We observed that under amino acid deprivation, SIRT2 knockdown increased ACSS2 acetylation levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SIRT2's deacetylation activity is specific to amino acid stress and not observed under glucose starvation.
source: Notably, this effect was not observed under glucose starvation, underscoring the specificity of SIRT2's deacetylation activity to amino acid stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: TM increased ACSS2 acetylation under amino acid-starved conditions but not under normal conditions.
source: TM increased ACSS2 acetylation under amino acid-starved conditions but not under normal conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using the SIRT2 inhibitor TM.

claim: The acetylation level of endogenous ACSS2 was increased by SIRT2 knockdown.
source: Furthermore, the acetylation level of endogenous ACSS2 was increased by SIRT2 knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Amino acid starvation triggers SIRT2 activation and subsequent deacetylation of ATG4B.
source: These findings align with a previous study demonstrating that amino acid starvation triggers SIRT2 activation and subsequent deacetylation of ATG4B (Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2022.

claim: SIRT2 deacetylates ACSS2 in response to nutrient stress, particularly amino acid deprivation.
source: Overall, our data indicates that SIRT2 deacetylates ACSS2 in response to nutrient stress, particularly amino acid deprivation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental data points showing SIRT2-dependent deacetylation under amino acid deprivation.

claim: Endogenous ACSS2 levels exhibited an increase upon SIRT2 knockdown in the presence of nutrient stress.
source: However, in the presence of nutrient stress, the endogenous ACSS2 levels exhibited an increase upon SIRT2 knockdown (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ACSS2 exhibited lower stability in the presence of amino acid limitation compared to normal culturing conditions.
source: We found that ACSS2 exhibited lower stability in the presence of amino acid limitation compared to normal culturing conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Under amino acid limitation, when SIRT2 is more active, there is an increased rate of deacetylation and degradation of ACSS2.
source: This suggests that under amino acid limitation, when SIRT2 is more active, there is an increased rate of deacetylation and degradation of ACSS2.
evidence: This is inferred from the stability data showing faster degradation under amino acid limitation.

claim: Under amino acid limitation, knocking down SIRT2 led to the stabilization of ACSS2.
source: Furthermore, our data demonstrated that under amino acid limitation, knocking down SIRT2 led to the stabilization of ACSS2 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: ACSS2 mRNA levels remained largely unaffected by SIRT2 knockdown or amino acid starvation.
source: Importantly, ACSS2 mRNA levels remained largely unaffected by SIRT2 knockdown or amino acid starvation (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: SIRT2-mediated deacetylation of ACSS2 under amino acid limitation promotes its degradation.
source: Overall, the data suggests that SIRT2-mediated deacetylation of ACSS2 under amino acid limitation promotes its degradation, revealing a potential mechanism by which nutrient stress modulates ACSS2 function.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on deacetylation, stability, and protein levels.

claim: Endogenous ACSS2 levels increased with MG132 treatment but not with Baf.
source: Endogenous ACSS2 levels increased with MG132 treatment but not with Baf, indicating that ACSS2 is degraded through the proteasomal pathway (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: ACSS2 is degraded through the proteasomal pathway.
source: Endogenous ACSS2 levels increased with MG132 treatment but not with Baf, indicating that ACSS2 is degraded through the proteasomal pathway (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of proteasome and lysosome inhibitors.

claim: Ubiquitination of Flag-ACSS2 was readily observed.
source: Moreover, we readily observed ubiquitination of Flag-ACSS2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Knockdown or inhibition of SIRT2 in amino acid deprived media led to a decrease in ACSS2 K48-linked ubiquitination.
source: Notably, we found that knockdown or inhibition of SIRT2 in amino acid deprived media led to a decrease in ACSS2 K48-linked ubiquitination (Figure 2F and G), a hallmark of proteasomal degradation, suggesting that SIRT2 regulates the ubiquitination and degradation of ACSS2 through the proteasome pathway (Kwon and Ciechanover, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: SIRT2 regulates the ubiquitination and degradation of ACSS2 through the proteasome pathway.
source: Notably, we found that knockdown or inhibition of SIRT2 in amino acid deprived media led to a decrease in ACSS2 K48-linked ubiquitination (Figure 2F and G), a hallmark of proteasomal degradation, suggesting that SIRT2 regulates the ubiquitination and degradation of ACSS2 through the proteasome pathway (Kwon and Ciechanover, 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the data on K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, supported by citation to Kwon and Ciechanover, 2017.

claim: ACSS2 acetylation levels at K271 increased in SIRT2 knockdown cells.
source: Utilizing label-free quantification mass spectrometry, we analyzed purified Flag-tagged ACSS2 from control and SIRT2 knockdown cells. Our analysis showed that ACSS2 acetylation levels at K271 increased in SIRT2 knockdown cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: SIRT2 knockdown failed to affect the acetylation level for the K271R mutant in amino acid deprived media.
source: SIRT2 knockdown failed to affect the acetylation level for the K271R mutant in amino acid deprived media, indicating that K271 is the site of deacetylation by SIRT2 (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: K271 is the site of deacetylation by SIRT2.
source: SIRT2 knockdown failed to affect the acetylation level for the K271R mutant in amino acid deprived media, indicating that K271 is the site of deacetylation by SIRT2 (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of SIRT2 knockdown on K271R mutant acetylation.

claim: The acetylation level of ACSS2 K661R mutant was still regulated by SIRT2.
source: In contrast, the acetylation level of ACSS2 K661R mutant was still regulated by SIRT2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: SIRT2 deacetylates ACSS2 at K271, which is different from previously reported SIRT1-regulated K661 deacetylation.
source: These observations collectively indicate that SIRT2 deacetylates ACSS2 at K271, which is different from previously reported SIRT1-regulated K661 deacetylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing K271 as the SIRT2 target site, distinct from K661.

claim: ACSS2 can be ubiquitinated at the K271.
source: Interestingly, data from the global characterization of the ubiquitin-modified proteome indicated that ACSS2 can be ubiquitinated at the K271 (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2011.

claim: K271R and K271Q mutants showed a decrease in ACSS2 ubiquitination levels.
source: To validate this, we tested the K48-linked ubiquitination of K271R and K271Q mutants, and both mutants showed a decrease in ACSS2 ubiquitination levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9.

claim: SIRT2 knockdown in amino acid deprived media decreased the ubiquitination of WT ACSS2, but not the ubiquitination of the K271R mutant.
source: SIRT2 knockdown in amino acid deprived media decreased the ubiquitination of WT ACSS2, but not the ubiquitination of the K271R mutant (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The K271R mutant exhibited enhanced stability compared to the wild-type (WT) ACSS2 when cells were cultured in EBSS medium lacking amino acids.
source: Furthermore, the K271R mutant exhibited enhanced stability compared to the wild-type (WT) ACSS2 when cells were cultured in Earle's balanced salt solution (EBSS) medium lacking amino acids (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Under amino acid limitation, SIRT2 deacetylates K271, thereby exposing the site for ubiquitination and leading to subsequent degradation of ACSS2.
source: Collectively, our findings suggest that under amino acid limitation, SIRT2 deacetylates K271, thereby exposing the site for ubiquitination and leading to subsequent degradation of ACSS2.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on deacetylation, ubiquitination, and degradation.

claim: Deletion of ACSS2 in mice results in reduced body weight and lipid deposition.
source: Deletion of ACSS2 in mice results in reduced body weight and lipid deposition, while mutation of S236, a phosphorylation site on ACSS2, leads to increased triglyceride levels in adipocytes (Huang et al., 2018; Shaik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2018 and Shaik et al., 2016.

claim: Mutation of S236, a phosphorylation site on ACSS2, leads to increased triglyceride levels in adipocytes.
source: Deletion of ACSS2 in mice results in reduced body weight and lipid deposition, while mutation of S236, a phosphorylation site on ACSS2, leads to increased triglyceride levels in adipocytes (Huang et al., 2018; Shaik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2018 and Shaik et al., 2016.

claim: The protein level of the K271R mutant was higher than that of the WT ACSS2 after 7 days of adipocyte differentiation.
source: After 7 days, we observed that the protein level of the K271R mutant was higher than that of the WT ACSS2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Re-expression of WT ACSS2 increased lipid accumulation based on Oil Red O staining of differentiated adipocytes.
source: In the ACCS2 knockdown cells, re-expression of WT ACSS2 increased lipid accumulation based on Oil Red O staining of differentiated adipocytes, thereby validating ACSS2's functional role in DNL.
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data.

claim: Expressing the K271R mutant lead to more lipid droplets than expressing the WT ACSS2.
source: Consistent with our above observation that ACSS2 K271R mutant is more stable than the WT, expressing the K271R mutant lead to more lipid droplets than expressing the WT ACSS2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inhibition of SIRT2 using TM increased lipid accumulation in cells with WT ACSS2, but not in cells with the K271R mutant.
source: The inhibition of SIRT2 using TM increased lipid accumulation in cells with WT ACSS2, but not in cells with the K271R mutant that cannot be deacetylated by SIRT2 (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: WT ACSS2 exhibits slightly higher activity compared to the K271R and K271Q mutants, but all variants remain functional.
source: Our findings indicate that while the WT ACSS2 exhibits slightly higher activity compared to the K271R and K271Q mutants, all variants remain functional (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: SIRT2 deacetylates ACSS2 on K271 to promote ACSS2 ubiquitination and degradation, and thus inhibiting lipogenesis.
source: These findings are consistent with the model that SIRT2 deacetylates ACSS2 on K271 to promote ACSS2 ubiquitination and degradation, and thus inhibiting lipogenesis (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data and supported by the working model in Figure 4.

claim: SIRT2-mediated ACSS2 K271 deacetylation only becomes obvious/important during nutrient (amino acid) limitation.
source: Interestingly, SIRT2-mediated ACSS2 K271 deacetylation only becomes obvious/important during nutrient (amino acid) limitation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects only under amino acid limitation.

claim: K271 deacetylation leads to the ubiquitination and degradation of ACSS2, resulting in reduced lipogenesis.
source: K271 deacetylation leads to the ubiquitination and degradation of ACSS2, resulting in reduced lipogenesis (see working model in Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and the working model in Figure 4.

claim: This regulatory mechanism can help to maintain cellular homeostasis by limiting lipogenesis under amino acid limitation.
source: This regulatory mechanism can help to maintain cellular homeostasis by limiting lipogenesis under amino acid limitation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: SIRT2 has been reported to be upregulated by several stresses, including Golgi stress caused by bacterial infection and nutrient depletion.
source: SIRT2 has been reported to be upregulated by several stresses, including Golgi stress caused by bacterial infection and nutrient depletion (Wang et al., 2022; Zullo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2022 and Zullo et al., 2018.

claim: SIRT2 is increasingly recognized as a stress response protein.
source: Thus, SIRT2 is increasingly recognized as a stress response protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the literature on SIRT2 upregulation under stress.

claim: Cells sense one metabolic stress (amino acid limitation) to regulate a different metabolic pathway (lipogenesis) by calling on SIRT2.
source: Our study here provides an interesting mechanism through which cells sense one metabolic stress (amino acid limitation) to regulate a different metabolic pathway (lipogenesis) by calling on SIRT2.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing SIRT2-mediated regulation.

claim: Dysregulation of DNL is associated with metabolic disorders such as obesity and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
source: Dysregulation of DNL is associated with metabolic disorders such as obesity and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: SIRT2 has been implicated in the regulation of DNL.
source: SIRT2 has been implicated in the regulation of DNL (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: SIRT2 is widely expressed in metabolically active tissues including adipose tissue.
source: SIRT2 is widely expressed in metabolically active tissues including adipose tissue and exerts its influence on DNL through the deacetylation of several proteins (Gomes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gomes et al., 2015.

claim: SIRT2 exerts its influence on DNL through the deacetylation of several proteins.
source: SIRT2 is widely expressed in metabolically active tissues including adipose tissue and exerts its influence on DNL through the deacetylation of several proteins (Gomes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gomes et al., 2015.

claim: During calorie restriction, SIRT2-mediated deacetylation of FoxO1 promotes its nuclear localization, where it suppresses the transcription of PPARγ.
source: During calorie restriction, SIRT2-mediated deacetylation of FoxO1 promotes its nuclear localization, where it suppresses the transcription of PPARγ, a master regulator of adipocyte differentiation (Wang and Tong, 2009; Hernandez-Quiles et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang and Tong, 2009 and Hernandez-Quiles et al., 2021.

claim: SIRT2-mediated degradation of ACLY decreases acetyl-CoA production, thereby inhibiting DNL.
source: SIRT2-mediated degradation of ACLY decreases acetyl-CoA production, thereby inhibiting DNL (Lin et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2013 and Guo et al., 2019.

claim: SIRT2 could also regulate another protein involved in DNL, ACSS2.
source: Our finding here revealed that SIRT2 could also regulate another protein involved in DNL, ACSS2.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: SIRT2 can inhibit DNL through deacetylating many different substrate proteins.
source: Thus, it seems that SIRT2 can inhibit DNL through deacetylating many different substrate proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple substrates of SIRT2 involved in DNL.

claim: Deacetylation of K661 by SIRT1 was found to activate ACSS2, leading to periodic increases in acetyl-CoA production.
source: Specifically, deacetylation of K661 by SIRT1 was found to activate ACSS2, leading to periodic increases in acetyl-CoA production (Sahar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sahar et al., 2014.

claim: SIRT2 inhibits ACSS2 by deacetylating K271 under conditions of nutrient stress.
source: Conversely, our research elucidates a contrasting mechanism wherein SIRT2 inhibits ACSS2 by deacetylating K271 under conditions of nutrient stress.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The dual regulation of ACSS2 by SIRT1 through the circadian clock and SIRT2 under nutrient stress underscores the intricate and multifaceted nature of regulatory mechanisms involved in lipid metabolism.
source: The dual regulation of ACSS2 by SIRT1 through the circadian clock and SIRT2 under nutrient stress underscores the intricate and multifaceted nature of regulatory mechanisms involved in lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of SIRT1 and SIRT2 regulation of ACSS2.

claim: GCN2 kinase, which responds to amino acid scarcity, regulates lipid metabolism by suppressing lipogenesis in response to amino acid deprivation.
source: For instance, Guo and Cavener found that GCN2 kinase, which responds to amino acid scarcity, regulates lipid metabolism by suppressing lipogenesis in response to amino acid deprivation (Guo and Cavener, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo and Cavener, 2007.

claim: There is an intricate interplay between amino acid metabolism and lipid metabolism.
source: This highlights the intricate interplay between amino acid metabolism and lipid metabolism, further emphasizing the significance of understanding the regulatory mechanisms involving enzymes like ACSS2 in various metabolic contexts.
evidence: This is inferred from the literature on metabolic regulation.

claim: DNL underlies many human diseases, including obesity and nonalcoholic liver disease.
source: DNL underlies many human diseases, including obesity and nonalcoholic liver disease (Yki-Järvinen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yki-Järvinen et al., 2021.

claim: Methods that can increase SIRT2 activity or protein levels may be useful for treating human diseases involving DNL.
source: Given the role of SIRT2 in suppressing DNL, methods that can increase SIRT2 activity or protein levels may be useful for treating human diseases involving DNL.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the role of SIRT2 in suppressing DNL.
